If you are aged 55 and above and looking to buy a short-lease 2-room Flexi flat or a Community Care Apartment (CCA), please refer to the section on [seniors](https://www.hdb.gov.sg/buying-a-flat/flat-grant-and-loan-eligibility/seniors).

answer.answer:
Yes, a married Singapore citizen and Singapore PR spouse can buy an HDB flat as an SC/SPR household. HDB’s family nucleus rules recognise a household where you are buying a flat as a Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident household, and for resale flats, any buyer or core family member who is an SPR must have held SPR status for at least 3 years at the time of the HFE letter application.[1][2]

For a new flat, the passages I have do not state the full flat types or detailed eligibility for an SC with an SPR spouse, so I couldn’t confirm more than that from the official sources I have.[1]

You should also note the property ownership rules. For buying a flat from HDB, all applicants and occupiers in the HFE application must not own or have an interest in any local or overseas private residential property, and must not have disposed of such property within 30 months before the HFE letter application.[1]

Apply for an HFE letter first, as it will state your eligibility to buy a new or resale flat and any housing support you may qualify for.[3] Please check the linked HDB page for the latest position.

answer.answer:
If you have already sold your private condominium, you may apply for an HFE letter to buy a new flat from HDB only after 30 months from the legal completion date of that sale. For example, if the legal completion of your condo sale was 1 July 2024, you may apply on or after 1 January 2027. This rule applies to buying a flat from HDB, or a resale Plus or Prime flat, and also to taking an HDB housing loan. [1]

There is a different rule for a non-subsidised resale unclassified/Standard flat (with or without Proximity Housing Grant), or certain short-lease flats from HDB. If you still own the private property at the time of your HFE letter application, you must dispose of it within 6 months after completing the flat purchase. [1]

So the key point is: for a new HDB flat, count 30 months from the legal completion date when you sold your private condominium before applying for the HFE letter. [1]

Do check the linked HDB page for the latest position before applying, as rules can change.

Wondering where to live next?

There are many different residential estates in Singapore, each with a unique flavour of its own. Estates are classified into mature or non-mature estates. In general, flats in non-mature estates are more affordable than those in mature estates. However, this phenomenon may change with the times.

**Mature Estates**

Ang Mo Kio, Bedok, Bishan, Bukit Merah, Bukit Timah, Central Area, Clementi, Geylang, Kallang/Whampoa, Marine Parade, Pasir Ris, Queenstown, Serangoon, Tampines, Toa Payoh

**Non-mature Estates**

Bukit Batok, Bukit Panjang, Choa Chu Kang, Hougang, Jurong East, Jurong West, Punggol, Sembawang, Sengkang, Woodlands, Yishun

At age 60, you may be able to buy a 3-room flat, but the options depend on whether you are buying alone or with someone else. The key thing I need to know first is your household type. [2][5]

If you are buying alone as a single Singapore citizen, the official singles rules say this applies to unmarried, widowed or divorced Singapore citizens aged 35 and above buying on their own. You should apply for an HFE letter first, as it will show your eligibility to buy a new or resale flat, and any CPF housing grants and HDB loan you may qualify for. [2]

If you are aged 55 and above, CPF’s guide says you can buy a short-lease 2-room Flexi flat from HDB, and you can also buy any flat in the resale market. That means a 3-room resale flat may be an option. [4]

For HDB loans, HDB says citizens aged 55 and above are eligible only if they are not applying for a 2-room Flexi flat on short lease. HDB loans are not available for short-lease 2-room Flexi flats or Community Care Apartments. [1]

If you are buying a resale flat, HDB also says you should check funds, lease-related CPF/loan restrictions, and get an HFE letter or bank Letter of Offer before proceeding. [6]

To narrow this down, I need to know: are you buying alone or with family/spouse, and are you looking at a new flat or a resale flat? [2][5]

A **Top-Up Grant** is not the usual grant for a first-time married couple. It applies if you previously received a Singles Grant or bought a 2-room or 2-room Flexi flat from HDB as a single and are now married. [2]

answer.answer:
You should plan for both cash and CPF at different stages of a resale flat purchase [2].

If you take a bank loan from a financial institution, at least 5% of the initial payment/downpayment must be paid in cash [1][2]. The remaining 20% of the downpayment can be paid using CPF savings [1].

You may use your CPF savings for the initial payment [2]. If you are taking an HDB housing loan, you and your co-applicant may each retain up to $20,000 in your CPF Ordinary Account, and the rest of the available OA balances must be used to pay for the flat purchase [2].

There are also cash payments to prepare for. If you intend to use CPF savings and/or a housing loan, you need to make a Request for Value unless otherwise advised by the financial institution, and the processing fee is $120 [2].

CPF also cannot be used for payments that need to be paid in cash, such as renovation [1]. Using more CPF may also mean a larger CPF refund later when you sell, which could reduce your cash sale proceeds [1].

answer.answer:
Plan for these upfront amounts when buying an HDB resale flat:

- **OTP deposit to the seller:** You pay an **Option Fee** when the OTP is granted and an **Option Exercise Fee** when you exercise it. The Option Fee is **$1 to $1,000**, and the total deposit (Option Fee + Option Exercise Fee) must not exceed **$5,000**. These amounts are negotiated with the seller and form part of the resale price. [4][5]

- **Resale application fee:** **$80**, or **$40 for 1- and 2-room flats**, when you submit your portion of the resale application. [2]

- **Request for Value fee:** If you intend to use **CPF savings and/or a housing loan**, you need to make a Request for Value to HDB, unless your financial institution advises otherwise. The processing fee is **$120**. [2]

- **Initial payment / downpayment:**
  - If you take a **bank / financial institution loan**, the minimum initial payment is **25% of the purchase price**, and **at least 5% must be in cash**. The rest of the initial payment may be paid using CPF savings. [1][2]
  - If you take an **HDB housing loan**, the minimum initial payment is **20% of the purchase price**, and it **can be fully paid using CPF Ordinary Account savings**. [1]

- **CPF housing grants:** If eligible, grants can be used for the **initial payment** and to reduce the housing loan amount. [2]

- **Remaining balance:** Any amount not covered by your initial payment, CPF grants, CPF OA savings and eligible housing loan must be paid **before or during the resale completion appointment**. [2]

I couldn't find a full list of other possible upfront items, such as the exact stamp duty amount, because the sources here only say prevailing stamp duties apply. Check the latest official pages before committing. [3]

How much CPF savings you can use for your home purchase

Learn more about the amount of CPF OA savings you can use to purchase a home.

*4 Aug 2025*

*SOURCE: CPF Board*

There is a limit on how much of your CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings can be used for a home purchase. This is so that you would have enough for your retirement.

This limit differs based on the valuation of the flat at time of purchase, purchase price, type of property, loan type, and age of property.

If the remaining lease of the flat can last the youngest owner until age 95, the amount of CPF savings you can use is capped at the lower of the purchase price and the valuation price at the time of purchase.

Your CPF savings can be used for purchasing a home, but did you know that there are limits in place?

Read on to learn more about using your CPF savings for a home purchase.

Part/Chapter: Part B

1. Use of CPF savings

a. You may use your CPF Ordinary Account (“**OA**”) savings for the following:

i. Direct payment of the purchase price of your private residential property to the property developer or sellers;

ii. Repayment of the housing loan in part or whole and/or to pay the monthly instalment of the housing loan taken for the purchase of your property, land and/or for construction of a house on that land; and/or

iii. Payment of the stamp duty, legal fees and other related costs incurred by you in connection with the purchase or mortgage of the property and/or construction of the house.

b. CPF savings cannot be used for the following:

i. Payment of option fees to property developers or sellers;

ii. Payment of construction works, improvements, repairs and/or renovation of your private residential property;

iii. Payment of monthly service and conservancy charges including all rates, taxes and other charges imposed on your private residential property;

iv. Repayment of non-housing loans (i.e. loans not taken for the purchase of your private residential property) and miscellaneous cost (i.e. penalties, insurance charges); or

v. Payment of purchase price that is above the lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for resale private residential property; and/or

vi. Reimbursement of any payments made to the property developers or sellers out of your personal funds in respect of the purchase of your private residential property.

Section: Terms and conditions for use of CPF under the CPF Housing Scheme > 1. Application of terms and conditions > Part B - Terms and conditions for use of CPF for private residential properties under the CPF Housing Scheme > 1. Use of CPF savings
Part/Chapter: Part B

1. Use of CPF savings

a. You may use your CPF Ordinary Account (“**OA**”) savings for the following:

i. Direct payment of the purchase price of your private residential property to the property developer or sellers;

ii. Repayment of the housing loan in part or whole and/or to pay the monthly instalment of the housing loan taken for the purchase of your property, land and/or for construction of a house on that land; and/or

iii. Payment of the stamp duty, legal fees and other related costs incurred by you in connection with the purchase or mortgage of the property and/or construction of the house.

b. CPF savings cannot be used for the following:

i. Payment of option fees to property developers or sellers;

ii. Payment of construction works, improvements, repairs and/or renovation of your private residential property;

iii. Payment of monthly service and conservancy charges including all rates, taxes and other charges imposed on your private residential property;

iv. Repayment of non-housing loans (i.e. loans not taken for the purchase of your private residential property) and miscellaneous cost (i.e. penalties, insurance charges); or

v. Payment of purchase price that is above the lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for resale private residential property; and/or

vi. Reimbursement of any payments made to the property developers or sellers out of your personal funds in respect of the purchase of your private residential property.

answer.answer:
Yes. CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings can be used to pay stamp duty and legal fees when buying a home under the CPF Housing Scheme.[1]

CPF states that OA savings may be used for the property purchase, downpayment, housing loan, and also “stamp and legal fees”.[1] For private residential properties, the terms also say OA savings may be used for “payment of the stamp duty, legal fees and other related costs” connected with the purchase or mortgage of the property and/or construction of the house.[3]

But there are limits on how much OA you can use for a home purchase. The amount depends on factors such as the property type, loan type and remaining lease, so you should check the official CPF housing usage calculator and the latest CPF page for your case.[2] CPF also says to balance OA use with cash and keep some OA savings for emergencies and retirement.[1]

Section: Looking for your retirement home > Additional information > How much CPF savings can be used

How much CPF savings can be used

CPF savings can be used for the purchase price, housing loan, stamp and legal fees.

If you are aged 55 and above and selling your current flat, the CPF refunds will first be used to top up your Retirement Account up to your Full Retirement Sum. The remaining refunds will be retained in your Ordinary Account.

You can check the amount available for use on your [Home ownership dashboard](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/homeownershipdashboard), including the exact amount that you would need to refund to your CPF account upon the sale of your current flat that can be reused for your next flat.

If you are buying a resale flat, use our [Housing Usage Calculator](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/tools-and-services/calculators/cpf-housing-usage) to estimate the amount of CPF savings you may use based on the flat's remaining lease.

Section: Mode of Financing for a Resale Flat > Use of CPF savings

**Retention of up to $20,000 in CPF OA**

Flat buyers taking a housing loan from HDB have the option of retaining up to $20,000 of the available [CPF savings](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/home-ownership/using-your-cpf-to-buy-a-home/retain-20000-in-your-oa-if-you-are-taking-a-housing-loan) in each buyer's OA. The remaining balance in the CPF OA must be used to pay for the flat purchase, before they can take an HDB housing loan. If you need the CPF refund from the sale of your current property to finance the resale flat purchase, please ensure the amount has already been credited to your CPF OA, before you submit the resale application.

**Conditions for use of CPF savings**

Take note of the following conditions for using your CPF savings:

There is a limit on the total amount of CPF savings that can be used for your flat purchase. Once that limit is reached, you will not be able to withdraw more of your CPF savings and have to pay the balance flat purchase price and/ or monthly mortgage instalments in cash

evidence.title: CPFB | T&C for use of CPF under CPF Housing Scheme
evidence.text:
Document: CPFB | T&C for use of CPF under CPF Housing Scheme
Section: Terms and conditions for use of CPF under the CPF Housing Scheme > 1. Application of terms and conditions > Part C - Standard terms and conditions > 2. Use of CPF saving for Multiple Property purchase
Part/Chapter: Part C

2. Use of CPF saving for Multiple Property purchase

a. There are additional restrictions if you have used your CPF savings for a property and are applying to use your CPF savings for a second or subsequent property (“**Multiple Property**”).

b. For Multiple Property bought from 1 July 2006 but before 10 May 2019:

i. You are required to set aside the latest BRS before you can use the excess savings in your OA for the Multiple Property;

ii. The maximum amount of CPF that can be used for your Multiple Property is capped at:

• Lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for property with a remaining lease of at least 60 years at the time of purchase; or

• A percentage of the lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for property with a remaining lease of less than 60 years but at least 30 years at the time of purchase.

c. For Multiple Property bought from 10 May 2019:

i. You are required to set aside the following before you can use the excess savings in your OA for the Multiple Property

• The latest BRS if you have at least one property bought using CPF or the property that you are buying can cover you till age 95*

• The latest Full Retirement Sum (“FRS”) if you do not have any property that can cover you till age 95

* If you subsequently sell the property that can cover you till age 95, you will need to set aside the FRS instead.

evidence.title: CPFB | How much CPF savings can I use for my property purchase?
evidence.text:
Document: CPFB | How much CPF savings can I use for my property purchase?
Section: FAQs

The amount of CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings you can use depends on:

Remaining lease of the property

Type of property

Loan type

Whether it’s your first or subsequent property

Note: For members age 55 and above, your Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) is [half of your Full Retirement Sum](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/article/how-much-is-my-basic-retirement-sum) (FRS) which depends on the year you turn 55 and will remain the same for life. For members below 55, your BRS is half of the prevailing FRS in the year.

You can use our [CPF Housing Usage Calculator](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/tools-and-services/calculators/cpf-housing-usage) to determine the total amount of CPF savings that you and your co-owner (if any) may use to buy your property.

CPF savings used to pay for stamp duty, legal fees and upgrading costs are not included in the CPF housing limit.

Purchasing your second or subsequent property

You can only use your OA savings after setting aside the BRS or FRS (refer to Table B), up to the CPF housing limit of your property.

Table B: Amount to set aside

answer.answer:
The key CPF restriction is this: for a second or subsequent property, you can use OA savings only after setting aside the required retirement sum first.[2][3]

Because you are 58, the missing facts that matter are:
- Is this your second or subsequent property using CPF? Extra restrictions apply only for multiple-property purchases.[2]
- When will you buy it? For multiple properties bought from 10 May 2019, you must first set aside the latest BRS if you already have at least one property bought using CPF, or if the property you are buying can cover you till age 95; otherwise you must set aside the latest FRS.[2]
- Do you currently have any property that can cover you till age 95, and will the new property do so? That decides whether the set-aside is BRS or FRS.[2]
- What is the remaining lease, property type and loan type? These affect how much CPF you can use.[3]

If you are 55 and above and buying a 3-room or smaller HDB flat, you may also use excess savings in your RA after setting aside your prevailing BRS.[5]

Also budget cash for items not payable with CPF, such as resale levy for a second subsidised flat, agent commission and renovation costs.[1]

I couldn’t find the exact BRS/FRS amounts or your CPF usage limit in the sources I have. You can use the CPF Housing Usage Calculator and Home Purchase Planner to check the latest position and retirement impact.[1][3]

evidence.title: CPFB | How much do I need to refund to my CPF account when selling/transferring my property?
evidence.text:
Document: CPFB | How much do I need to refund to my CPF account when selling/transferring my property?
Section: FAQs

To check the exact amount that you need to refund your CPF accounts if you sell/transfer your property, simply log in to your [Home ownership dashboard](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/homeownershipdashboard) and look under the “What Happens If” section.

In general, the amount you must refund is the principal you have withdrawn for your property (P) and the accrued interest (I), i.e. “P+I”. If you are age 55 or above and have pledged your property to set aside your retirement sum, you must also refund the pledged amount.

**IMPORTANT NOTE:**

However, please note that your required CPF refund is less than your P+I if you:

were age 55 or older before 1 January 2013; and

have set aside your Full Retirement Sum (FRS) before 1 January 2013.

This is because having set aside your FRS before 1 January 2013, you are not required by law to refund the CPF you have used to pay for your property prior to 2013. If you have continued to use your CPF from 1 January 2013, only the principal amount used from 1 January 2013 and the accrued interest need to be refunded when you sell your property.

answer.answer:
The key CPF restriction is this: for a second or subsequent property, you can use CPF Ordinary Account savings only after setting aside the required retirement sum, up to the CPF housing limit for that property [1].

Because you are age 55 and above, the retirement sum test uses your own cohort’s Basic Retirement Sum or Full Retirement Sum, which stays the same for life [1]. CPF also says members 55 and above can check on the Retirement Dashboard whether they have set aside their Full Retirement Sum [2].

What matters next is whether you own a property in Singapore with a remaining lease that lasts you until age 95 or older. If yes, you may apply to withdraw Retirement Account savings down to your BRS [2]. If not, I couldn’t find in the sources I have that you can rely on this option [2].

Other CPF limits for the new home also depend on facts not given here: the remaining lease of the property, the type of property, the loan type, and whether this is your first or subsequent property [1].

If you will sell or transfer your current property, CPF refund rules matter too. In general, you must refund the principal withdrawn plus accrued interest, and if you are 55 or above and pledged the property to set aside your retirement sum, you must also refund the pledged amount [3]. Check the linked official dashboards/calculator for your exact position [1][2][3].
